C004.subject: overall immigration
C004.object: negligible net effect on native workers' wages when accounting for dynamic adjustments
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: overall immigration negligible net effect on native workers' wages when accounting for dynamic adjustments]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of immigration wage effects with dynamic adjustments (e.g., Peri & Sparber, 2009; Ottaviano & Peri, 2012; Dustmann, Schönberg & Stuhler, 2016) — Aggregates decades of empirical studies that separate short-run partial equilibrium from long-run general equilibrium effects, directly testing whether net wage impact is negligible after accounting for capital deepening and specialization.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic general equilibrium simulation calibrated to U.S. economy (e.g., extended Bewley-Huggett-Aiyagari model with heterogeneous agents, immigration, and endogenous capital accumulation) — Simulates multi-decade adjustments in capital stock, occupational mobility, and firm response, quantifying whether aggregate native wage effects converge to near zero, thus refuting or confirming the hypothesis under standard assumptions.

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment exploiting sudden immigration shocks (e.g., 1980 Mariel boatlift, 1990s Albanian inflows to Italy) with long-term panel data on native wages and local capital formation — Provides causal identification of wage effects over decades, allowing observation of dynamic adjustments (e.g., capital inflows, native out-migration) and testing if eventual net effect is negligible.

qualifier.methodological_controversy: general equilibrium adjustment (capital inflows, specialization) neutralizes partial equilibrium impacts

C005.subject: immigration of low-skilled workers
C005.object: short-term wage increases or no reduction for native low-skill workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of low-skilled workers short-term wage increases or no reduction for native low-skill workers]

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment using the Mariel Boatlift (1980) as an exogenous shock to low-skilled labor supply; re-analyze with modern difference-in-differences methods on individual-level wage data for native low-skilled workers in Miami vs. comparison cities. — This classic case provides a quasi-experimental setting to test short-run wage effects. Replication with more robust controls and longer panels can confirm whether the original finding of no wage reductions holds under modern methods, addressing the substitution effect controversy.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on low-skilled immigration and native wages in local labor markets, focusing on short-run (0-5 years) effects, with stratification by sectoral concentration and labor market tightness. — Given the disputed status, a systematic quantitative synthesis across many studies and locations can reveal the average effect size, heterogeneity, and conditions under which wage increases or no reduction occur, clarifying the methodological controversy.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching dynamic model of local labor market with task-specific complementarities between immigrant and native low-skilled workers, calibrated to US metropolitan data. — A model incorporating adjustment frictions, firm entry, and sectoral mobility can explain how short-run local equilibria might yield modest wage increases or no reduction despite a dominant substitution effect, offering testable predictions for empirical design.

qualifier.methodological_controversy: substitution effect dominant in local equilibrium
